extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public and aspiring writers/essayists
extracted.subtask_description: Short-form literary guidance and exemplars for composing epitaphs, brief character portraits, and observational sketches—with advice on tone, physiognomic detail, narrative reliability, and depiction of grief and social manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaph style: diffused (luxuriant) vs contracted (close)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The first being in the diffused and luxuriant, the second in the close contracted Style. The first has much of the Simple and Pathetick; the second is something Light, but Nervous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two contrasting models for epitaph-writing are presented and exemplified: (a) a longer, diffusely rhetorical, pathetic/solemn form (sample: the Thomas Sapper epitaph with extended family history and lament), and (b) a short, concise, witty form (sample: 'Here lies the Body of Daniel Saul, Spittle-fields Weaver, and that's all.'). Use the former for pathos and memorial detail, the latter for economy, wit, or a mordant effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaph that withholds praise / invites ultimate judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Here lieth R. C. in expectatione diei supremi. Qualis erat dies iste indicabit.' — Here lieth R. C. in expectation of the last Day. What sort of a Man he was, that Day will discover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A powerful epitaphic device is refusal of biographical praise: present the deceased and defer moral judgement to a future or divine moment. This ironic/reflective turn can be serious and highly effective; the essayist lauds it as 'in my Opinion, the finest that I ever met with upon this Occasion.' Use when you want restraint, moral ambiguity, or to provoke readers' reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of physiognomy as shorthand for character/profession
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a very close Correspondence between the outward and the inward Man ... The Practitioners in this Art often make use of a Gentleman's Eyes to give 'em Light into the Posture of his Brains; take a Handle from his Nose, to judge of the Size of his Intellects; ... a contracted Brow, a lumpish down-cast Look, a sober sedate Pace ... is Logick, Metaphysicks and Mathematicks in Perfection. ... a Saunter in the Gate; a Fall of one Wing of the Peruke backward ... is typified the Belles Lettres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sketching characters, deploy concrete external markers (posture, gait, dress, facial features, habitual gestures) as signals of temperament, learning, or profession. The passage provides explicit mappings (e.g. contracted brow + sedate pace → logician; saunter + peruke + pinch of snuff → belle-lettrist; open breast + audacious display → soldier). Use such cues to economize characterization and to make types immediately recognizable; beware of crude stereotyping, but employ these details as effective shorthand in brief sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show non-verbal cues; do not rely solely on reported words
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The force of the Expression lies very often more in the Look, the Tone of Voice, or the Gesture, than the Words themselves; which being repeated in any other Manner by the Undiscerning, bear a very different Interpretation from their original Meaning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reporting scenes or reconstructing events, foreground non-verbal behavior (looks, tone, gestures). Written retellings that omit these cues risk misrepresenting the original meaning. The author also counsels scepticism toward 'Matter of Fact' tellers—eyewitness accounts are prone to embellishment—so writers should preserve ambiguity or indicate how delivery altered sense. Examples in the text illustrate how narration escalates from credible detail to Marvelous to Impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict social manners with precise, modest physical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Good Breeding obliges a Man to maintain the Figure of the keenest Attention, the true Posture of which in a Coffee-house I take to consist in leaning over a Table, with the Edge of it pressing hard upon your Stomach; for the more Pain the Narration is received with, the more gracious is your bending over.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, concrete physical gestures (a particular lean, the pressing of a table edge, a tilt of the peruke) efficiently evoke setting and social codes. Use such modest, specific details to lend verisimilitude and to signal character attitude (attention, affectation, dissembling) without long exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish narrator-types: embellishers vs reciters
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Of these Liars there are two Sorts. The Genius of the first consists in much Impudence and a strong Memory; the others have added to these Qualifications a good Understanding and smooth Language. These therefore have only certain Heads, which they are as eloquent upon as they can, and may be call'd Embellishers; the others repeat only what they hear from others as literally as their Parts or Zeal will permit, and are called Reciters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or reporting contemporary social characters, classify and render different modes of falsehood: (a) embellishers—creative narrators who add color and inventiveness; (b) reciters—faithful but credulous repeaters. Differentiating these types allows the writer to dramatize social transmission of rumor and to control narrative reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character through small actions, bequests, and funerary rituals
rubrics_metrics.description: The butler's letter details Sir Roger's bequests (pearl necklace to his lady, gelding to the chaplain, books to friends), the distribution of mourning clothing, the tenants carrying the coffin, and the pall held by members of the Quorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than explicit eulogy, disclose a person's values and relations through inventory (gifts, bequests), ritual behavior, and the responses of others at death (who carries the coffin, who wears mourning). These concrete particulars function as indirect characterization and produce emotional effect—use them to show rather than tell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray grief as a morally revealing mixture of equanimity and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is a certain Equanimity in those who are good and just, which runs into their very Sorrow, and disappoints the Force of it ... that very Affliction shall add Force to their Integrity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict mourning as complex: virtuous sorrow can temper violent passion into gentler compassion and refined sensibility. Effective portrayals combine outward signs (tears, withdrawing, physical faintness) with inward reflection (memory of kindness, conversion of temper). Use such contrasts to render grief believable and morally charged; avoid caricatures of unfeeling stoicism or overwrought, aimless melodrama.
